ext.title: Cross-Industry Political Spending -- Analysis (Overview memo)
ext.venue: Unattributed internal memo, dated 12/10/2025 (TO, FROM and CC names redacted). Not a peer-reviewed or published academic work.
ext.document_type: Unattributed internal analysis memo (unpublished). Metadata hint confirmed: memo, names redacted, dated 12/10/2025.
ext.coverage: Full text read (51 lines, about 14.4k chars, single chunk). Redactions: all personal and some organization names are blacked out as BBBB. The entire Case Study section (lines 29-33) is redacted and gives no findings. One sentence in the Charles Schwab paragraph (line 26) is partly redacted. No annotation or markup files were listed for this item, so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: Whether executive and corporate political spending in four industries (life insurance, mutual funds, credit unions, commercial banking; top 10 by revenue each) is offloaded onto company executives, and whether these industries adapt their giving to executive-branch pressure and scrutiny "regardless of party" (Overview, line 11).
ext.theory: No formal theory is stated. The memo's framing is that firms adapt campaign finance to risk and scrutiny from the executive branch (lines 11, 20, 40, 43). Centralized coordination is presented as a way to avoid a prisoner's dilemma (line 36, mentioned without citation). Splitting donations across opposing candidates is described as risk mitigation (line 47).
ext.data: Top 10 companies by revenue in each of four industries (about 40 firms, implied; the memo does not give an explicit N). Units: individual CEO and executive contributions, company PACs, trade associations (ACLI, American Credit Union trade association "ACU", American Bankers Association), and the four biggest Super PACs (House Majority PAC and Senate Majority PAC are named). Period: "cyclical" averages over unspecified election cycles ("both cycles" in the insurance section, "past 3 election cycles" for credit unions, "several cycles" for banks). Dated references run from 2021 to Nov 2025 (Schwab charity investments 2021-2024; JPMorgan memos June 2024 and June 2025; Dimon interview Nov 2025). Sources are described only as "publicly available" and "publicly disclosed" (lines 18, 22). No database, filing source, or contribution-level N is named.
ext.method: Descriptive only. Per-industry averages of CEO and executive spending in dollars. Trade association average donations and cumulative industry PAC totals. Ratios of outside giving to PAC giving (life insurance, line 16). Share of Super PAC money originating from the company rather than individuals (JPMorgan, +90%, line 21). Qualitative characterization of year-to-year volatility (line 25) and partisan split (lines 24, 40-42). Qualitative review of internal memos, employee communications, interviews, and news reports of DOJ and executive-order actions.
ext.identification: None. No comparison group, statistical test, or design that supports causal claims. The link between executive-branch scrutiny and giving rests on timing and narrative (lines 19, 26-28), with hedged wording such as "most likely" (lines 22, 28).
measures: Average annual CEO spending in dollars, by industry
Average annual executive spending in dollars, by industry
Average trade association donation in dollars (ACLI, ACU, ABA)
Cumulative industry PAC spending in dollars
Annual average Super PAC spending in dollars (insurers, mutual funds)
Outside-to-PAC spending ratio (CEO and executive, life insurance)
Share of Super PAC donations originating from the company rather than individuals
ext.scope: Population: top 10 companies by revenue in life insurance, mutual funds, credit unions, and commercial banking. Institutions: US federal political giving through company PACs, trade associations, Super PACs, and candidate contributions. Era: the current Trump administration as described in the memo (DOJ investigations, executive orders), with reference to the prior Biden administration (line 28) and 2021-2025 events.

key_findings.finding: Memo states that spending is offloaded onto executives and that industries respond to executive-branch pressure regardless of party. Stated as confirmation of an 'original assumption'. No numbers in this paragraph.
Life insurance: CEO average spending and executive average spending across the top 10 firms. Ranked 3rd of four industries in raw spending.
Life insurance donations to the trade association ACLI are called disappointing and rank lowest in PAC size.
key_findings.numbers: ACLI CEO avg $3,000; executive avg $1,166; ACLI PAC avg $911,470

key_findings.finding: Insurers rank 2nd in Super PAC spending. Memo says the figure includes health and other insurance, and that most money comes from individuals tied to companies, not the companies.
Life insurance giving is drifting toward individual outside donations, not company PAC or trade association. CEOs give $1.15 outside per $1 to PAC; executives give $1.54 to PAC per $1 outside.

Commercial banking: CEOs rank 1st in raw spending per the memo, but most of it goes to company PACs. Several CEOs give nothing directly to candidates, including Moynihan (Bank of America) and Masrani (TD Bank).
Bank of America shows rising PAC spending and a more balanced partisan split, which the memo ties to Moynihan's silence after the debanking dispute and the DOJ investigation.
JPMorgan: internal memos pushed PAC giving, and the company streamlined PAC donations. More than 90% of donations to House Majority PAC and Senate Majority PAC come from the company, not individuals.
key_findings.numbers: +90% of House and Senate Majority PAC donations originate from the organization

key_findings.finding: American Bankers Association is 2nd in overall spending among trade-association giving named in the banking section. Memo concludes banks are avoiding direct contributions and taking a nonpartisan route.

Mutual funds: CEO and executive averages and a trade association average, ranked 3rd in trade association investment. Memo says the apparent average spending is a facade, with the real spending channeled into Super PACs.
key_findings.numbers: CEO avg $17,882; executive avg $83,990; trade association avg $966,875

key_findings.finding: Mutual fund industry PACs total about $13M, while the four biggest Super PACs receive an annual average of about $261M, mostly to GOP-aligned groups. Memo calls this a vast reservoir of partisan spending.
key_findings.numbers: industry PACs cumulative $13M; four biggest Super PACs annual avg $261M

key_findings.finding: Mutual fund year-to-year spending is the most volatile of the four industries.

Charles Schwab: the company PAC and executives halted donations, but Chairman Schwab and his wife redirected giving to a charity fund that the memo says invested over $250M (2021-2024) in conservative causes and gave to Republican Super PACs. The memo links this to later Trump-administration roles and a $250M+ investment in a Trump-branded startup.

Credit unions: lowest CEO and executive averages of the four industries, which the memo attributes to smaller industry revenue. Coordination through the ACU trade association (news bulletin board, member outside-giving allowance, in-state restriction for non-member PACs) is presented as offsetting this.

Credit unions report $0 dark money to the four biggest Super PACs and a near-perfect bipartisan ratio (no figure given). Behaviour includes big donations to open seats and special elections and hedging by giving to the opposing candidate when maxed out on a challenger.
key_findings.numbers: $0 dark money to four biggest Super PACs

key_findings.finding: Case Study section is fully redacted and yields no findings.

limitations: Data sources, sample sizes, cycle years, and data-collection method are not stated. The memo relies on 'publicly available' and 'publicly disclosed' spending (lines 18, 22) without citation.
The memo itself says displayed spending 'reveals an incongruence with the true scale' of industry spending (line 25), so the disclosed figures are acknowledged as incomplete.
Life insurance Super PAC figure includes health and other insurance, so it is not specific to life insurers (line 15).
Causal claims (executive-branch pressure drives giving) rest on timing and news narrative, with hedged language ('most likely', lines 22, 28). No test or control group.

Internal ranking inconsistencies: commercial banking is called 1st in CEO raw spending at $16,781 (line 18), while mutual funds' CEO average is $17,882 (line 24) and is described as '1nd' (likely a typo for 1st). Life insurance is ranked 3rd in raw spending (line 13). The rankings are not reconciled.
The 'regardless of party' claim (line 11) sits uneasily with the memo's own finding of GOP-aligned Super PAC money in mutual funds (line 25). The memo does not reconcile this.

Several quantities are approximate or unsupported: 'near perfect' bipartisan ratio (line 42) has no figure, 'many CEOs' and 'several CEOs' give no counts, and the life insurance trajectory toward outside giving is described but not quantified (line 16).
The 'original assumption' and 'original hypothesis' (lines 11, 13) are referenced but never stated in the text.
The Case Study section and parts of the Schwab paragraph are redacted, so claims that depend on them cannot be checked.
The memo cites no academic literature. The prisoner's dilemma (line 36) and the 'hive mind' analogy (line 36, drawn from a TV show) are used without citation.

short_quotes.quote: spending is being offloaded onto company executives
we have to be very careful about how anything is perceived
we have to be emotionally disciplined, and recognize that we will not win divided
short_quotes.location: Credit Union, line 36 (ACU CEO, as quoted in memo)

rel.summary_md:
An unsigned internal memo dated 12/10/2025. Names are redacted and it is not peer-reviewed. It profiles federal political giving by the top 10 firms by revenue in four industries: life insurance, mutual funds, credit unions and commercial banking. It splits that giving across CEOs, other executives, company PACs, trade associations (ACLI, ACU, ABA) and the four largest Super PACs. Its headline claim is that firms push political spending onto executives and adjust their giving to executive-branch scrutiny "regardless of party". The evidence is per-industry dollar averages, which carry no cycle years, source or N, plus news-driven case stories: Bank of America after the DOJ probe, JPMorgan's PAC memos, and the Schwab charity fund. There is no comparison group and no test. The memo reports its own ranking contradictions, and it uses "dark money" to mean Super PAC money.

For Paul's systems the memo is a descriptive input, not evidence. Its unit of analysis is the same one Mentat's spending-statistics sheet already builds. That sheet has role tiers (Chief, Middle Management, Employee, Corporate) and channel columns (Super PAC, Company PAC, Trade Association, Candidate, Company PAC to Super PAC, each with a partisan split). Mentat also ingests a "Credit Union Cross Industry Spending.xlsx" template. The memo may therefore come from the same product line, and if it does it is not an independent check. Two parts are useful. First, the bank, mutual-fund and CU stories show giving moving into channels that per-member models never see: trade associations, Super PACs, and family or charity vehicles. That bears on how Melange's flip model measures competitor money. Second, its partisan readings of Super PAC money ignore whether the money supported or opposed a candidate, which Mentat already separates. Every figure in the memo should be treated as UNVERIFIED, with no window or denominator.

bearings.paper_claim: Bank CEOs give little directly to candidates (several give nothing, e.g. Moynihan, Masrani). Bank money flows through company PACs and the ABA (cyclical average $2,402,499). Mutual-fund money is said to be 'channeled into Super PACs' (industry PACs about $13M cumulative versus about $261M annual average at the four biggest Super PACs). CU giving runs through ACU coordination, with $0 reported to the four biggest Super PACs.
bearings.paper_location: Commercial Banking lines 18-22; Mutual Funds lines 24-25; Credit Union lines 36-42
bearings.system_side: The flip model's competitor-money leg b is fed by ind0 = banks + finserv, the PAC-to-member contribution columns in congestion.json. CU money is the cu column. Trade-association dollars, Super PAC independent expenditures for or against a member, and executives' individual giving never enter a or b. If the memo's channel picture holds, the b-term understates bank and fund pressure exactly where those industries avoid direct giving.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This carries over only as a structural caution. The memo's dollar figures have no stated source, cycle window or N, and some may be industry totals rather than per-member amounts. It shows no member-level allocation, so it cannot recalibrate WM or HALFF. Before any engine change, Mentat's own Super PAC and trade-association columns would need to be mapped to members.

bearings.paper_claim: Mutual-fund Super PAC money goes 'mostly to GOP-aligned groups' ('a vast reservoir of partisan spending'). Over 90% of JPMorgan-linked House Majority PAC and Senate Majority PAC donations come from the company rather than individuals. Credit unions report '$0 dark money' to the four biggest Super PACs.
bearings.paper_location: Mutual Funds line 25; Commercial Banking line 21; Credit Union lines 41-42
bearings.system_side: Mentat splits entity (Corporate) contributors from persons. It reports 'Company PAC: To Super PAC' with a partisan split, and it walks PAC-to-PAC-to-candidate transfers by date (F12). It keeps 527 and 501(c) money as separate supplementary categories rather than calling Super PAC money dark money. The brain records that 89% of beneficiary dollars were oppose-coded, so the destination committee's alignment does not equal support for that party's candidates. The memo reads partisanship from the destination group alone.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Federal FEC data from the same era; the industries overlap the CU and banking work. The memo's partisan and 'dark money' readings should not be quoted against Mentat output unless they are recomputed with the support/oppose partition and the 501(c)/527 distinction. The attributed-estimate producer is unbuilt, so Mentat cannot yet give the downstream split either.

bearings.paper_claim: Charles Schwab's company PAC and executives stopped giving. Per the memo, the Chairman and his wife moved their giving to a charity fund that invested over $250M in conservative causes from 2021 to 2024 and gave to Republican Super PACs. The memo's thesis is that spending is 'offloaded onto company executives', measured as CEO and executive averages per industry.
bearings.paper_location: Overview line 11; Mutual Funds line 26 (partly redacted)
bearings.system_side: Mentat assigns individual receipts to a company by employer string (strict names: roster plus verified aliases). It assigns role tiers from the executives roster or from title regex: CEO, CFO, GC, founder, owner, chairman and president count as Chief; VP, director and manager count as Middle Management. Money a chairman routes through a family or charity vehicle is attributed only if that vehicle's own filings name the employer, and the 501(c) category is supplementary.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The extension is to link executive-controlled vehicles (foundations, donor-advised funds, family LLCs) to the roster person. It would need a verified-affiliation rule consistent with the strict-names policy, never a fuzzy guess. The memo's 'executive' definition is unstated, so its averages cannot be reconciled with the Chief or Middle Management tiers.

bearings.paper_claim: Industries adapt their giving to executive-branch pressure 'regardless of party'. Examples: Bank of America's rising PAC spending and more balanced partisan split after the debanking dispute and DOJ probe, and JPMorgan streamlining its PAC after internal memos. The causal link is hedged ('most likely').
bearings.paper_location: Overview line 11; Commercial Banking lines 19-22; Mutual Funds line 28
bearings.system_side: The SHIFT family regresses industry partisan share on expected-minus-current House and Senate control, with a presidential-year term and wild sector-cluster bootstrap with Holm adjustment. It found no stable partisan shift (-0.04, p .76). It has no regressor for executive-branch scrutiny events such as DOJ actions or executive orders aimed at an industry.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The memo's claim concerns the executive branch, while SHIFT concerns congressional control, so the two do not test the same thing. The memo's evidence is firm-level anecdote with no counterfactual. At most it motivates a pre-registered event study around dated enforcement actions. It cannot be cited as a finding.

bearings.paper_claim: Credit unions have the lowest CEO and executive averages of the four industries (CEO $5,147, executive $3,009). Their giving is coordinated through the ACU trade association, with near-perfect bipartisan balance (no figure given), open-seat and special-election emphasis, and hedging across opposing candidates.
bearings.system_side: The CU company-PAC measure is the published panel's 16-PAC cohort, with the D/R split pinned from that same cohort (D-117). Individual-executive giving is not the forecast unit for CUs.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This loosely supports treating CU political money as PAC- and association-led, so the panel cohort rather than executive giving is the right unit. Neither the 'near-perfect' bipartisan ratio nor the volatility claims come with figures, so they cannot be used to check the pinned split.

gaps_exposed: Melange's flip and break-even money legs see only direct PAC-to-member dollars (cu, banks + finserv). Trade-association and Super PAC independent-expenditure money targeted at a member is absent, and the memo argues those are the main bank and mutual-fund channels.

Mentat has no linkage from roster executives to their personal or charitable vehicles (foundations, donor-advised funds, family entities). Giving that an executive redirects off the employer field goes unattributed.
No study variable captures executive-branch enforcement or scrutiny events (DOJ probes, executive orders). The sector-growth SHIFT tests cover congressional control only.

No figure for within-industry volatility of giving by channel. The memo calls mutual funds the most volatile, which bears on forecast interval width, but the forecast reports no per-industry dispersion.
flags: UNVERIFIED (DE-062): every dollar figure in the memo lacks a source, cycle window, N and denominator, which breaks the rule that every figure names its window and denominator. Quote none of them without that label.

The memo may not be independent of the system. Its channel and role layout matches Mentat's spending-statistics sheet (report.R:64-80), and Mentat ingests a 'Credit Union Cross Industry Spending.xlsx' template (ingest.R:1294). If it was built from Mentat output, it cannot serve as a second path that reproduces Mentat.
Terminology conflict: the memo calls Super PAC donations 'dark money'. Mentat keeps Super PAC money (FEC-disclosed) separate from 501(c) and 527 money. Do not import the memo's wording.

The memo's partisan readings of Super PAC money ignore support/oppose direction, and the brain records that 89% of beneficiary dollars were oppose-coded. 'GOP-aligned' destinations do not equal pro-GOP spending.

The causal claim (executive-branch pressure drives giving 'regardless of party') rests on narrative and timing. It sits uneasily with the memo's own GOP-tilted mutual-fund finding, and its ranking contradictions are unreconciled (bank CEO $16,781 called 1st, below the mutual-fund CEO's $17,882).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this memo. It loosely agrees with his reading of strategic, cycle-aware giving (Bacik: more money in election years; Furnas: party-tied firms lose when that party loses). It also agrees with his wish to map rival industries (banks and funds against CUs). But it supplies only industry averages and anecdotes, with no member-level allocation. It cannot answer his 'conflicting industries' note for the industry boards or the flip model. The system's own SHIFT result found no stable partisan shift with expected control. That cuts against generalizing the memo's 'adapt to whoever holds power' story, though the memo concerns the executive branch, which SHIFT does not test. If Paul or his team wrote this memo, its framing of channel substitution is now better covered by Mentat's role and channel columns and the support/oppose partition than the memo's own figures. The memo should be read as a framing document, not as evidence.

related.why: Cross-industry finance and lobbying report under Paul's name on the same subject (industry political spending across finance sectors). It may share data lineage with this memo; that is unverified because this memo's names are redacted.

Furnas et al. show low overlap between organizations' lobbying and PAC spending. That supports the memo's premise that money moves across separate channels, and warns against treating any single channel as an industry's total effort.
Irvin investigates real dark money (nonprofit 501(c) advocacy). That corrects the memo's use of 'dark money' for disclosed Super PAC donations.
Couch et al. model a dark-money transfer network. That is the network view the memo's Super PAC 'reservoir' claim would need, and it parallels Mentat's PAC transfer graph.
Kim et al. link firm-level donations to lobbying using executive and employee giving matched to firms. That is the rigorous version of the memo's executive-offloading measurement.
